solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Luxury material silver miners extract

indicators.note: to extract is to draw something out from inside, so the letters come from within the words that follow

parts.note: running across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Miners digging silver out of the ground to make luxury goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extract' reads as a verb for what miners do, but it signals letters taken from inside silvER MINErs.
explanation.definitionFit: The white winter fur of the stoat, traditionally trimming royal and judicial robes, is a costly prestige fabric.

clue.text: Keep on turning up at pub, disheartened

parts.note: re means on, concerning

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning upward makes the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: losing one's heart means losing the middle letter of the word

parts.note: an inn is a pub

explanation.surface: Someone who keeps turning up at the pub, fed up with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep on' looks like one phrase meaning continue; only 'Keep' is the definition, and 'on' supplies RE. INN without its middle N leaves IN.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep something is to hang onto it and not let it go, a straightforward verb synonym.

clue.text: Circles unevenly scratched in rocks

indicators.note: the uneven, odd-numbered positions are scratched out, so only the even-numbered ones survive

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Rough circular scratches found gouged into rock faces.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing C, R, L and S from CIRCLES leaves the even letters I, C, E.
explanation.definitionFit: Rocks is slang for ice cubes in a drink, as in whisky on the rocks.

clue.text: Leisure centre to rally support for art

parts.note: ease is leisure, freedom from work

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letter, so only that one is taken

parts.note: the middle of the five letters

explanation.surface: A leisure centre being used to drum up backing for the arts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leisure centre' reads as a sports building, but the words split: Leisure gives EASE and 'centre' works on 'rally'.
explanation.definitionFit: A painter's wooden stand holds the canvas upright while a picture is being worked on.

clue.text: Unending fight to save very sick author

indicators.note: to save something is to keep it safe inside, so one piece is held within another
without an ending, the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a melee is a confused fight
V is the abbreviation for very
ill means sick

explanation.surface: A never-ending battle to rescue a writer who is gravely ill.
explanation.walkthrough: MELEE loses its final E to give MELE, which then holds V and ILL.
explanation.definitionFit: Herman Melville was the American novelist who wrote Moby-Dick, so he is an example of a writer.

clue.text: Examination claimed to be fixed

indicators.note: something that must be fixed is broken and needs putting back together in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone alleging that a test or exam was rigged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fixed' suggests rigged, but here it means rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor's physical check-up of a patient is commonly called by this noun in British usage.

clue.text: Prominent position of land bearing fruit

indicators.note: in a down clue, bearing something means carrying it on top, so that piece comes first

parts.note: a lime is a citrus fruit
to light is to land, as a bird lights on a branch

explanation.surface: A prime spot of ground where fruit grows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Land' looks like a noun for ground, but it is the verb, meaning to come down and settle.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in the public eye, the centre of attention, comes from the bright stage lamps once used in theatres.

clue.text: River turning south into English Channel eventually

indicators.note: turning into something means changing into it, so one letter becomes another

parts.note: the Indus is a great river of Pakistan
S is the abbreviation for south
E is the abbreviation for English
a course is a channel along which water flows

explanation.surface: A river that swings south and finally empties into the English Channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English Channel' reads as the sea between England and France, but the words split; the Indus is the great river of Pakistan, whose final south-letter turns into an English one.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means at the proper time, sooner or later, which is an idiom for finally.

clue.text: Trouble over children covering current affairs

indicators.note: in a down clue, whatever covers another lies on top of it and comes first
turned over means flipped round, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: to ail is to trouble
I is the symbol for electric current
sons are children

explanation.surface: Worry about children being exposed to news and politics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current affairs' reads as news, but current gives I and affairs alone is the definition; I sits above SONS in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Illicit romantic relationships, especially secret love affairs, are known by this French-borrowed word.

clue.text: Fools, perhaps backtracking under pressure

indicators.note: going back over one's tracks means travelling in the opposite direction

parts.note: a fool is a fruit-and-cream pudding, so fools are an example of puddings

explanation.surface: Foolish people who back down when put under pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: A fool is a British dessert of puréed fruit folded into cream, and 'perhaps' marks fools as one kind of dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling anxious strain and tension from demands is what being worried and overloaded means.

clue.text: Someone nosy sounding out fruit

indicators.note: sounding something out means saying it aloud, so the word is judged by its sound

parts.note: a meddler pokes a nose into other people's business

explanation.surface: A busybody going round asking about fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounding out' looks like questioning someone, but here it means saying a word aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a small brown apple-like tree fruit eaten when half rotten, so an example of the category.

clue.text: Mixing lab acid with oil could be fiendish

indicators.note: mixing stirs things together so they end up in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A chemistry warning: combining lab acid with oil could be devilishly dangerous.
explanation.walkthrough: The ten letters of the three middle words are rearranged, and 'could be' simply links them to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something devilish, wicked or cruel, as if the work of Satan himself.

clue.text: Who minds small charges?

parts.note: surface reading: who objects to paying minor fees or bank fees
setter's reading: to mind is to look after, and charges are the young children in someone's care

explanation.walkthrough: 'Minds' looks like 'objects to' and 'charges' like fees; both switch meaning, to looking after little ones placed in someone's care.
explanation.definitionFit: People paid to watch over youngsters while parents are out look after little wards, the children entrusted to them.

clue.text: Time to avoid pithy language

indicators.note: to avoid something is to leave it out, so a letter is removed

parts.note: terse means pithy, brief
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: It is time to stop using short, snappy wording.
explanation.walkthrough: TERSE without its T; Erse is an old name for Scottish or Irish Gaelic.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gaelic tongue of the Scottish Highlands or Ireland has this older name, common in crosswords.

clue.text: British PM once almost crushed in war zone

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter is cut

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for British
Clement Attlee was the postwar Labour Prime Minister
crushed means ground, as coffee is

explanation.surface: A former British Prime Minister nearly killed in a war zone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crushed in' suggests a container, but crushed simply gives GROUND and the pieces run in order.
explanation.definitionFit: A field of combat where armies fight is another way of naming a region of warfare.

clue.text: One rubbish bitter served up by a bistro

indicators.note: in a down clue, sent upward means read from the bottom back to the top

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
rot means nonsense, rubbish
tart means sharp-tasting, bitter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pint of awful bitter beer served in a little bistro.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bitter' looks like the beer, but it is the adjective sour.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the Italian word for a simple, informal restaurant, much like a small French café.

clue.text: Prospect of gold being found in a country

indicators.note: something found inside another thing is enclosed by it

parts.note: Panama is a Central American country
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: The chance of striking gold in some country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prospect of gold' reads as prospecting, but Prospect is the definition, meaning view.
explanation.definitionFit: A prospect can mean a wide, sweeping view over the landscape, an unbroken scene in every direction.

clue.text: Valet's sniggering gives offence

parts.note: a valet is a manservant, a man, and the apostrophe S is kept
sniggering is a kind of laughter

explanation.surface: A manservant's giggling upsets his employer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Offence' looks like hurt feelings, but it is a crime; a gentleman's valet is traditionally called his man.
explanation.definitionFit: Unlawful killing without malice aforethought is a serious crime, a legal wrongdoing short of murder.

clue.text: Making money from a gulf in supply

indicators.note: supply can be read as the adverb from supple, so the letters bend into new shapes

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Profiting from a gap between what is supplied and what is wanted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is both fodder and part of the signal; 'supply' is the adverb of supple, meaning flexibly.
explanation.definitionFit: Work that pays wages or is profitable is described with this adjective, as in gainful employment.

clue.text: Derelict roadhouse cleaned out by maid

indicators.note: cleaning out empties the inside, so only the outer letters stay

parts.note: first and last letters
a maid is a young woman, a miss

explanation.surface: A run-down roadside inn scrubbed clean by the housemaid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Derelict' looks like it describes the roadhouse, but it is the definition, as in derelict in one's duty.
explanation.definitionFit: Being negligent, failing in one's duties or responsibilities, is the sense shared by both words.

clue.text: Plane, for one rolling in money

indicators.note: something rolling turns over, so the letters come round the other way

parts.note: a plane is a woodworking tool, so an example of one

explanation.surface: An aeroplane, say, as something a rich person owns when rolling in money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plane' suggests an aircraft, but it is the carpenter's smoothing tool; 'rolling in money' is a phrase that must be split.
explanation.definitionFit: Loot is informal slang for cash, as well as for stolen goods and plunder.

clue.text: Final items of work eaten by dogs

indicators.note: whatever is eaten ends up inside the eater

parts.note: to dog someone is to follow them closely, to tail them
a piece is a work, as of art or music

explanation.surface: The last pieces of homework chewed up by the dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dogs' reads as animals, but it is the verb, meaning follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Ornamental pieces or appended sections placed at the end of a book or chapter conclude it.

clue.text: Fruit, soft and fleshy

parts.note: a plum is a fruit
p (piano) means soft in music

explanation.surface: A description of fruit that is soft and juicy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soft and fleshy' reads as a pair of adjectives for the fruit, but soft gives the musical P.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a body or shape that is rounded and well-padded, pleasantly chubby.

clue.text: Rush job

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to hurtle along out of control
second meaning: a lifelong profession or line of work

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rush job' looks like hasty work, but the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to speed wildly, and as a noun it means a person's working occupation.

clue.text: Female unit on a camouflaged jet

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for female

indicators.note: camouflage disguises a thing's form, so the letters are rearranged to hide them

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An all-women military squad aboard a disguised fighter plane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unit on a' looks like connecting words, but all seven letters are the fodder, and jet is water, not aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: A spout of water forced up into the air is a jet, the kind seen in ornamental garden displays.

clue.text: A couple that's overly outspoken

indicators.note: spoken out means said aloud, so the word is judged by its sound

parts.note: too means overly, excessively

explanation.surface: A pair of people who speak their minds far too freely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overly outspoken' reads as one phrase, but overly supplies the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A couple is a pair, which is simply the number coming between one and three.

clue.text: He planned reconstruction entirely on wetlands

indicators.note: in an across answer, one thing placed on another comes after it, so the earlier-named piece goes second

parts.note: a marsh is wetland
all means entirely, wholly

explanation.surface: A developer drew up rebuilding plans over marshy ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points to the Marshall Plan, the American programme that funded the rebuilding of Western Europe after the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: George C Marshall, the US Secretary of State, devised the Marshall Plan to rebuild Europe's postwar economies.

clue.text: Writer for American leader on trial

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
US is short for American

indicators.note: the leader of anything is at the front, so only the first letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: An author writing for a US president facing trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American leader' suggests a president, but American gives US and leader works on trial.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcel Proust was the French novelist who wrote In Search of Lost Time, an example of an author.
